KEY MESSAGES:

-  Summer-like conditions through Thursday with highs in the 80s,
   90s in lower valleys of north-central Idaho. 

-  Isolated showers and thunderstorms increase in coverage by
   Thursday and Friday. 

-  Dramatic shift to colder and wetter this weekend. Hypothermia
   risk. Higher elevations will be "Winter-like" with Snow 
   accumulation possible down to 6000-7000 feet.
 
-  Return to a summer-like, thunderstorm pattern by the start of
   July. 
   
On the satellite loop this morning, there was a plethora of 
wildfire smoke seen over Utah and Colorado. Closer to home, there 
are several wildfires located in central Washington and within 
our forecast area there is the Shingle Creek Fire, located 
northwest of Pollock, Idaho. The latest smoke forecasts keep much
of north-central Idaho and western Montana out of the smoke for 
the next several days. By Thursday, the flow becomes more 
southwesterly which may bring some increased smoke into the 
region, generally seen as a haze in the mountains. Hopefully the 
incoming wet system this weekend will help douse some of those 
fires!

A few showers or a thunderstorm may fire off the terrain in
Glacier National Park this evening, but with the warm advection
occurring aloft that should help to stabilize things. 

On Wednesday, we begin to see shortwave energy starting to move
around the flat ridging in place. The chance for precipitation has
been increased, especially in the terrain across western Montana.
Any storms will be weak, but still lightning and gusty winds 
could be impactful. 

By Thursday, the surface trough begins to shift into western
Montana and at the same time a decent upper level disturbance will
trigger more showers and thunderstorms. The Lifted Indices(LI) 
become more negative, signifying stronger buoyancy or lift in the
atmosphere. While cloud cover and storms developing earlier than
max daytime heating could limit instability, there could be a few
storms that are able to grow tall enough to produce hail greater 
than 0.50" and allow charge separation for more lightning. The 
wind shear is weak, so these mountain-initiated storms may be 
more short-lived and unorganized. Instability (CAPE) values could 
be approaching 500-700 J/KG, especially across northern Lake and 
Flathead Counties which would be supportive of tall growth and the
aforementioned hail and lightning threats.
 
More shower activity is expected Friday as the cold front moves 
through. Winds gusting to 35 mph are possible across Lemhi 
County. Expect cooler conditions and more cloud cover which will 
limit greater instability. There could be enough unstable 
conditions to trigger a few storms over the Divide, southwest 
Montana, towards southern Lemhi County and areas south and east of
Grangeville.

Then a very cold low pressure system from the Gulf of Alaska will
drop down over the Pacific Northwest by Saturday. This will cause
snow levels to fall to 7000-8000 feet by Saturday morning. It will
be much cooler with highs in the 50s and 60s. This system has some
similar features to a cut-off low that swung across Idaho on June
29, 2020. That system brought multiple inches of rainfall from
Idaho County east and north into Montana. It also brought snow
down to 6000 feet, several inches to Lost Trail Pass and impacted
a trail crew in Lemhi County who were stuck in 8 inches of snow 
in the high country for a period. Forecast snow levels have been 
trended downwards. This system poses a hypothermia risk for those 
in the backcountry. You may want to keep a saw or chainsaw handy 
in case the snow/rain brings down a tree and blocks the road. One
way that this system may be different from the 2020 event is the 
fact that some model solutions are developing a secondary low with
wrap- around precipitation across northwest Montana Sunday into 
Monday. We're looking at 60-80% probability for widespread 0.25" 
of precipitation or greater. For probabilities exceeding one inch 
of precipitation, the Clearwater Mountains in Idaho have a 60-80%
chance, and the Mission Mountains to Glacier National Park have a
60 to 75% chance of occurrence.

The NBM and recent ensemble systems depict our region becoming
under warm, southwest flow with a trough centered near Vancouver
Island by the start of July. This would place us back into summer
and also would be conducive for thunderstorms.
